title: First Sentence Only
learningGoals: Separate the opening from the whole answer

deeperExplanation.question: What if my first sentence is not the best one?
deeperExplanation.answer: It needs to be useful enough to begin, not the best possible sentence. A listener can ask a follow-up, and you can clarify what you mean. If you are introducing a project, a plain sentence about its purpose is often sufficient. Trying to discover the ideal opening can keep you at the doorway. Starting with a real meaning lets the conversation help shape the next part.

sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring First Sentence Only. Before answering, you try to organise the entire explanation, choose perfect wording and protect every possible difficult word. The answer feels too large to begin.

In this session, we will separate the opening from the whole answer, choose one useful first sentence, and let the next sentence develop. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: First Sentence Only reduces the immediate task. Decide what the first sentence needs to do, say it, and let the next sentence be shaped by what follows. You are not abandoning the message. You are allowing it to unfold in manageable pieces. The first sentence may state the main point, answer a small part or ask for clarification.

sections.narration:
Before answering, you try to organise the entire explanation, choose perfect wording and protect every possible difficult word. The answer feels too large to begin.

It is possible to know your direction without preparing every word. Think of the listener’s question and choose a starting meaning. If you need a pause afterwards, you can take one. If the listener asks a question, the next sentence may change. This flexibility is part of conversation, not a failure of preparation.

What if my first sentence is not the best one?

It needs to be useful enough to begin, not the best possible sentence. A listener can ask a follow-up, and you can clarify what you mean. If you are introducing a project, a plain sentence about its purpose is often sufficient. Trying to discover the ideal opening can keep you at the doorway. Starting with a real meaning lets the conversation help shape the next part.

sections.narration: Use a first-sentence intention before one everyday answer. Notice what became possible after you began. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
